concepts.name: Article 368: Scope and Nature of Amending Power
key_dimensions: Whether Article 368 confers a constituent power or ordinary legislative power — distinction matters for Basic Structure scrutiny
Shankari Prasad vs Golak Nath evolution: Can 'law' under Article 13 include constitutional amendments?
Article 368(1) vs 368(2): difference between procedure and substantive power to amend
UPSC trap: Article 368 says 'Parliament may amend by way of addition, variation or repeal' — does this include implied limitations?

concepts.name: Three-Tier Classification of Amendment Procedures
key_dimensions: Tier 1 — Simple majority (outside Article 368 scope): Articles like creation of new states, salaries of MPs, quorum rules
Tier 2 — Special majority (2/3rd present and voting + majority of total membership): Core constitutional provisions
Tier 3 — Special majority + ratification by at least half of State Legislatures: Federal provisions listed in Article 368 proviso
UPSC trap: Simple majority amendments are NOT under Article 368 — they are ordinary legislation; confusing these three tiers is a classic error

concepts.name: Special Majority Requirement: Exact Constitutional Formula
key_dimensions: Must satisfy BOTH conditions simultaneously: (a) 2/3rd of members present and voting AND (b) majority of total membership of each House
Difference from ordinary special majority used in other contexts (e.g., removal of judges, UPSC members)
UPSC trap: 'Total membership' means full sanctioned strength, not just those present — absence reduces effective threshold
No provision for joint sitting under Article 368 — deadlock between Houses cannot be resolved by joint session

concepts.name: Ratification by State Legislatures: Scope and Mechanics
key_dimensions: Only specific provisions require state ratification — Article 368 Proviso lists them exhaustively: election of President, extent of executive/legislative power of Union and States, Supreme Court, High Courts, representation in Parliament, Article 368 itself
UPSC trap: 'At least half the State Legislatures' — no time limit prescribed for ratification unlike some other countries
State Legislatures ratify but cannot initiate or veto independently; Parliament's role remains primary
Whether ratification can be withdrawn once given — constitutionally untested but relevant for MCQ traps

concepts.name: Provisions Amendable by Simple Majority (Outside Article 368)
key_dimensions: Key list: Admission of new states (Art.2), formation of new states (Art.3), citizenship rules (Art.11), 5th and 6th Schedule amendments in certain cases, abolition of Legislative Councils, quorum in Parliament
UPSC trap: These are amended by ordinary legislative process — President's assent required but NOT special majority or state ratification
Salaries of constitutional functionaries amended by simple majority — commonly tested
Distinction: Parliament acting as ordinary legislature vs Parliament acting as constituent assembly under Art.368

concepts.name: Basic Structure Doctrine: Origin and Core Holdings
key_dimensions: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): 13-judge bench; 7:6 majority established Basic Structure — Parliament cannot abrogate the Constitution's identity
Concept not explicitly in text — judicially evolved implied limitation on Article 368
UPSC trap: Basic Structure restricts only constitutional amendments under Art.368, NOT ordinary legislation (which is tested under Part III directly)
Doctrine applies prospectively — past amendments not automatically invalidated; courts examine on case-by-case basis

concepts.name: Elements of Basic Structure: Judicially Identified Features
key_dimensions: Core elements from various cases: Supremacy of Constitution, Republican and democratic form, Secular character, Separation of powers, Federal character, Judicial review, Free and fair elections, Rule of law, Parliamentary system, Unity and integrity of India
UPSC trap: Basic Structure list is NOT exhaustive and NOT codified — courts continue to identify new elements (e.g., 'right to vote' debated in PUCL case)
Distinction: Preamble is part of Constitution but 'socialist', 'secular' added by 42nd Amendment — their basic structure status is debated
Harmony Doctrine: Directive Principles vs Fundamental Rights — Art.31C and its validity tested through Basic Structure lens

concepts.name: Article 13 vs Article 368: The Law-Amendment Conflict
key_dimensions: Article 13(2): State shall not make any 'law' that abridges FR — does 'law' include constitutional amendment?
Shankari Prasad (1951): Constitutional amendment is NOT 'law' under Art.13 — Parliament can curtail FRs
Golak Nath (1967): Overruled Shankari Prasad — constitutional amendment IS 'law', cannot abridge FRs
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Overruled Golak Nath — amendment is not 'law' under Art.13 BUT Basic Structure limitation applies; Art.368(3) inserted to nullify Art.13 explicitly

concepts.name: 24th, 25th, 42nd, and 44th Constitutional Amendments: Legislative Responses to Judicial Rulings
key_dimensions: 24th Amendment (1971): Affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part including FRs; amended Art.13 and Art.368 to clarify
25th Amendment (1971): Inserted Art.31C — laws giving effect to DPSP (Art.39b/c) not void for violating Art.14, 19 — challenged and partially upheld in Kesavananda
42nd Amendment (1976): Attempted to make amendments non-justiciable; added Art.368(4) and (5) — struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)
44th Amendment (1978): Restored Art.19(1)(f) deletion, Right to Property moved to Art.300A — UPSC trap on which amendment abolished FR of property

concepts.name: Minerva Mills Case (1980): Judicial Review as Basic Structure
key_dimensions: Struck down Art.368(4) and (5) inserted by 42nd Amendment — Parliament cannot make its amending power unlimited
Held: Judicial review and harmony between FRs and DPSPs are Basic Structure — unlimited expansion of Art.31C (as amended) unconstitutional
Key principle: Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme — amending power is limited constituent power, not sovereign power
UPSC trap: Minerva Mills confirmed Kesavananda's Basic Structure but went further by striking down explicit constitutional text — rare instance

concepts.name: Waman Rao Case and Doctrine of Prospective Overruling
key_dimensions: Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981): Kesavananda applies prospectively — amendments before April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) not re-examined for Basic Structure
Doctrine of Prospective Overruling: Originated in Golak Nath — new rule applies only to future cases; unusual in Indian jurisprudence
UPSC trap: Prospective overruling means earlier 9th Schedule laws get immunity from Basic Structure challenge if inserted before 1973
IR Coelho case (2007) partially modified this for 9th Schedule — post-1973 additions can be judicially reviewed

concepts.name: Ninth Schedule and Constitutional Amendments: IR Coelho Case
key_dimensions: 9th Schedule (added by 1st Amendment 1951): Laws placed here immune from FR challenge — originally to protect land reforms
IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007): 9-judge bench — laws added to 9th Schedule after April 24, 1973 can be judicially reviewed if they violate Basic Structure/essential FRs
UPSC trap: 9th Schedule is NOT a blanket immunity — post-Kesavananda insertions are now reviewable; this is a commonly tested nuance
Currently 284 laws in 9th Schedule — any new addition now risks judicial scrutiny

concepts.name: Role of President in Constitutional Amendment Process
key_dimensions: Article 368(2) proviso: After passage by both Houses, presented to President — President 'shall give his assent'
24th Amendment made assent mandatory — President has NO power to withhold assent to Constitution Amendment Bills (unlike ordinary bills under Art.111)
UPSC trap: President cannot return a Constitution Amendment Bill for reconsideration — pocketveto and suspensive veto both unavailable
Contrast with ordinary bills: President has three options; for Constitution Amendment Bills, only one option — assent

concepts.name: No Joint Sitting Provision for Constitutional Amendment Bills
key_dimensions: Article 108 provides for joint sitting to resolve deadlock between Houses — but explicitly NOT applicable to Constitution Amendment Bills
If Rajya Sabha rejects or passes with amendments unacceptable to Lok Sabha — the bill lapses; no mechanism to override
UPSC trap: Joint sitting is available for ordinary bills and Money Bills procedure is different — Constitution Amendment Bills stand alone
Rajya Sabha's equal power in constitutional amendments makes it more powerful here than in Money Bills or ordinary legislation

concepts.name: Initiation of Constitution Amendment Bills: Houses and Ministers
key_dimensions: Article 368(2): Amendment can be initiated in EITHER House of Parliament — unlike Money Bills (only Lok Sabha)
Can be introduced by any member — not restricted to ministers; private member Constitution Amendment Bills are permissible
UPSC trap: No provision for introduction in State Legislatures — unlike in USA where states can call constitutional conventions
Both Houses must independently pass with special majority — there is no concept of one House having primacy

concepts.name: Federalism and Constitutional Amendments: Centre-State Dimension
key_dimensions: India's amendment procedure is less federal than USA (where 3/4th states must ratify most amendments) — Indian states' role is limited to specific provisions
State Legislatures' ratification: Simple majority sufficient — no special majority required from states, unlike Centre
UPSC trap: State Legislatures ratify but Parliament can proceed without waiting indefinitely — no time limit for state ratification creates asymmetry
SR Bommai case and federalism as Basic Structure — limits Centre's power to fundamentally alter federal balance through Art.368

concepts.name: Distinction: Constitutional Amendment vs Ordinary Legislation — Practical Overlaps
key_dimensions: Some constitutional provisions can be changed by ordinary law (e.g., jurisdiction of Supreme Court under Art.138 expanded by Parliament by simple majority)
UPSC trap: Creating or abolishing a state Legislative Council (Art.169) requires ordinary special majority in Parliament + resolution by state assembly — NOT under Art.368
Delimitation, citizenship rules, election procedures — appear constitutional but amended by ordinary statute
Anti-Defection Law (10th Schedule) added by 52nd Amendment — amendable under Art.368 but originally debated as ordinary legislation

concepts.name: Constitutional Amendments and Judicial Review: Scope After Kesavananda
key_dimensions: Post-Kesavananda: Courts can strike down constitutional amendments — this power itself is part of Basic Structure (Minerva Mills)
Standard of review: Courts examine if amendment 'abrogates or abridges' Basic Structure — not mere violation but fundamental damage
UPSC trap: Courts cannot examine the 'wisdom' or 'policy' behind an amendment — only its constitutional validity vis-à-vis Basic Structure
Recent applications: NJAC judgment (2015) struck down 99th Amendment — collegium system as part of Basic Structure (independence of judiciary)

concepts.name: 99th Amendment and NJAC Judgment (2015): Recent Application of Basic Structure
key_dimensions: 99th Constitutional Amendment established National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) replacing collegium system
Supreme Court in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015): 4:1 majority struck down 99th Amendment
Held: Independence of judiciary and primacy of judiciary in appointments is Basic Structure — executive participation in NJAC violated it
UPSC trap: The Amendment was passed with special majority AND ratified by more than half of state legislatures — yet struck down; demonstrates limits of formal compliance with Art.368 procedure

concepts.name: Amendment of Fundamental Rights: Historical and Current Position
key_dimensions: Current settled position (post-Kesavananda): Parliament CAN amend FRs but CANNOT abrogate or destroy the core/essence of FRs as that would violate Basic Structure
Right to Property: Removed from FR list by 44th Amendment (1978) — moved to Art.300A as constitutional right; UPSC trap on which amendment and its current status
Art.21 expansions through judicial interpretation vs Parliament's power to curtail — living document tension
Triple Talaq Act and Art.25 — ordinary legislation vs constitutional amendment route; UPSC tests on choosing correct legislative path
